newsitem.title: GERMANY: Dollar drives German DAX bulls to record close.
newsitem.headline: Dollar drives German DAX bulls to record close.

text.p: Germany's DAX index ended bourse trade at a record closing high on Wednesday, keeping up Tuesday's steamrollering bull run, with the sturdy U.S. dollar the main engine driving gains and no correction in sight.
The DAX index ended bourse trade at 3,364.99 points, up 44.33 points or 1.33 percent, just a whisker off an all-time high hit during the session of 3,365.03 points.

"There are some decent volumes there and the greenback is helping, especially with the exporters. The slogan at the moment seems to be -- enjoy it and let the cash roll in," said Josh Waiblinger of equity sales at BHF Bank in Frankfurt.

Dealers expressed admiration at the market's bullish resilience in the face of some less than inspirational fundamental factors, which hardly indicated a vigorous recovery but did quell most fears of inflation.
These included sluggish German GDP data, downbeat January industrial orders, a lower Wall Street overnight and a softer German debt market.

The strength of the dollar at 1.71 marks, at or around 34 month highs and seemingly unstoppable at the moment, was viewed by market players as a panacea for any wobbles, woes or potential jitters in the German share market.
The market shrugged off worries of unspectacular economic growth after fourth quarter Gross Domestic Product figures showed only a 0.1 percent rise, up 2.2 percent from the year-earlier quarter.

What could have been a double whammy for the market came with further bad news on the macroeconomic front after German January industry output figures showed a 1.7 percent drop, mainly driven by a 25 percent month-on-month drop in the construction industry.
Again, the market took this in its stride in mid-session bourse and the market stayed steady.
Earlier factors included a nearly one-percent lower close on the Dow Jones Index overnight and downbeat German debt all contributed to early fears of a consolidation, if not a full-blown correction.

Dealers breathed a sigh of relief when early electronic trade on the IBIS DAX index was stable. "If a correction was going to happen it probably would have happened by now," said one Frankfurt trader.
Indeed, early lacklustre electronic trade early on soon turned to another assault on record highs when the index hit 3,349.94 points.

Wild fluctuations up or down barely raise an eyebrow in Frankfurt these days. "100 point shifts have almost normal. This kind of volatility is definitely not as shocking as it was a couple of years ago," said Waiblinger.
Waiblinger said it was also possible that caution in the United States could be seeing some funds moving over to Europe, which would boost the German stock market.
Shares in the limelight included Deutsche Lufthansa AG, which ended up 5.09 percent at 24.17 marks.
Traders had identified a large domestic buyer who was buying "massive" amounts of the stock. The stock was lifted by a Boeing report which forecast a 4.4 percent increase in air travel in Europe.
Diversified utility Veba AG was also higher at end-bourse, up 1.40 marks at 99.40 marks, as technical factors buoyed the stock.
Tyre-maker Continental AG ended floor trade up one mark at 34.80 marks after it said its 1996 pre-tax profits were up 68.2 percent at 328 million marks.
